newsitem.title: USA: PSE&G sees $5.5 bln of stranded costs.
newsitem.headline: PSE&G sees $5.5 bln of stranded costs.

text.p: Public Service Electric and Gas Co now estimates its stranded costs total $5.5 billion, Corporate Rate Council Francis Delany said on Monday.

He told a news conference these costs include $1.6 billion for contracts the company has with non-utility generators and $3.9 billion of costs of generation assets the company believes will be stranded in a competitive market.

As PSE&G said in a statement earlier, its filing Tuesday with New Jersey regulators will include a request that it be allowed to securitize $2.5 billion of the $3.9 billion of generating assets it believes will become stranded.
That filing is being made in response to an order issued by April by the state's Board of Public Utilities.
Securitization at that level is expected to result in a 2.3 percent rate reduction, Delany said.
This would be part of the five to 10 percent reduction the utility promises in its filing, he explained.

He pointed out the board has already said utilities can recover the costs associated with the non-utility generators' contracts, adding this will be done as part of PSE&G's distribution costs over the 10 to 15 year life of these contracts.
Delany said the company expects the bonds sold to refinance its generation assets under the securitization process will have a life of 15 years.
He also said PSE&G will attempt to recover the remainder during the seven year transition to a competitive market called for in the utility's restructuring proposal.
The $3.9 billion of estimate of stranded costs is based on the company's expectation of market prices over the transition period, Vice President Marketing Fritz Lark said.
The amount compared with PSE&G's electric production assets of $6.0 billion at the end of 1996, President Lawrence Codey says in testimony prepared for Tuesday's board meeting.
The actual "amount of the price reduction will be dependent on the outcome of negotiations and decisions reached" as the board considers the utilityu's proposal, the testimony continues.

"Included in these key elements are securitization levels, non-utility generation contract reformation, changes in depreciation, certainty of electric and gas allocation factors for rate making pourposes, a seven-year transition period and demand side management cost recovery," he said.
Codey told reporters Monday the company is seeking depreciation flexability from the board, but provided no specifics.

He plans to tell the board PSE&G's ability to reduce rates on January 1, 1999, and cap them for a seven-year transition period, "is directly linked to the successful conclusion and execution of the securitization ... proposal.

"In the event the enabling legislation is not enacted or that securitization does not proceed, it would not be possible to resolve transition costs within the eight-year timeframe suggested by the board in (its) restructuring report."

He said the company's proposal to freeze rates for seven years makes it responsible for the risk of inflationary increases in fuel and operating and maintenance costs; "and we will take the full risk of mitigation and absorption of non-securitized generation assets" totaling $1.4 billion.

At the end of that transition period, Lark said, the company expects to have all costs at market levels except for the continuing contracts with non-utility generators and payment of the bonds used to securitize stranded costs.
